summary: Describes a method for setting up and keeping SNA sessions over an IP internet, carrying IBM Systems Network Architecture traffic across IP networks.

plainLanguage.summary: Two old computers speak their own language. This memo shows how to send their conversation through the Internet in a sealed envelope.

questions: how does sna work over tcp
subtitle: Carrying IBM network traffic through the Internet

tldr.problem: IBM Systems Network Architecture (SNA) was traditionally tied to token-ring networks, but organizations needed a way to send SNA traffic across IP networks and the Internet.
tldr.mechanism: Advanced SNA/IP uses UDP datagrams to negotiate a connection between two SNA nodes, then establishes a TCP connection to carry the actual SNA session data with minimal overhead.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can now route SNA sessions over IP networks, though with a modest 15% performance cost compared to token-ring.

facts.label: Connection negotiation method
facts.value: UDP datagrams (Logical Null XID, XID Request, Logical SNA XID)

facts.label: Data message framing
facts.value: Two-octet big-endian length field before each SNA message

today: RFC 1538 is an Informational RFC, not a standard. It documents the Advanced SNA/IP approach as implemented in specific gateway products. SNA itself is now largely obsolete as organizations have migrated to TCP/IP-native applications, though this RFC remains a record of how legacy systems were made routable.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This RFC documents a method for transporting Systems Network Architecture (SNA), IBM's proprietary network protocol, over IP networks. Traditionally, SNA sessions relied on token-ring networks and logical link control (LLC), a link-layer protocol designed for reliability and ordering. Advanced SNA/IP enables SNA nodes like gateways and downstream nodes to communicate via TCP/IP, making SNA routable across the Internet.

The protocol was originally implemented in products like the McDATA LinkMaster and I/O Concepts TN3270 servers. Unlike some earlier SNA-over-IP schemes, this design can work not just in peripheral network nodes but also in intermediate routers, making it viable for building IP-based SNA switches.
sections.plainLanguage: This explains how to send IBM SNA messages through the Internet. SNA was built for local networks, so this adds a wrapper that makes it work over the public Internet.

sections.title: Why SNA Needed to Cross IP Networks
sections.content:
For years, McDATA and other vendors implemented SNA over token-ring (802.5) and later over Ethernet (802.3) using LLC. These work well within a local network, but LLC frames do not route across the Internet. As organizations installed IP networks and expected them to handle all traffic, the question arose: can SNA run over routable IP?

TCP running over IP provides the reliable, ordered delivery that SNA requires, plus the routing capability that LLC lacks. Advanced SNA/IP was created to replace LLC type I and type II services with UDP and TCP, giving SNA sessions the ability to traverse IP routers and the Internet itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Companies had SNA working on local networks but wanted it to cross the Internet. TCP is reliable and routable, so the designers used it to carry SNA conversations.

sections.title: The Three Phases of Connection
sections.content:
The Advanced SNA/IP protocol divides a session into three phases. The first is Connection Establishment, which negotiates parameters between two SNA nodes using three UDP datagrams: a Logical Null XID sent by the initiating node (like a downstream node asking to connect), an XID Request from the partner (usually an SNA gateway), and a Logical SNA XID containing SNA-level configuration data. Once these exchanges agree on parameters, a TCP connection is established.

The second phase is Data Transfer. Once TCP is open, SNA messages flow as TCP segment data, each preceded by a two-octet (big-endian) length field. No special framing or SNA/IP protocol is added; the SNA message format is unchanged. TCP handles all reliability and ordering.

The third phase is Connection Termination. Either node may send a TCP FIN segment to cleanly close the session. If a FIN is not received (for example, if the downstream node fails), the gateway may not know the connection is gone; to handle this, reconnecting nodes must reuse the same TCP port so the gateway recognizes when a reset is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: First, the two computers exchange UDP messages to agree on how to talk. Then TCP opens. They send SNA messages down the TCP connection with a simple length header. Finally, one sends a close signal and TCP shuts down.

sections.title: Packet and Message Structure
sections.content:
Connection establishment uses three types of UDP datagrams, each carrying just a one-byte marker (0xBF) or SNA XID data. The Logical Null XID and XID Request are identical in format; they differ only in direction and role (DSN initiates, gateway responds). Each includes the source and destination IP addresses and ports.

For data transfer, each TCP segment containing SNA data is prefixed with a two-octet length field in big-endian format. The length counts the SNA message (transmission header, request/response header, and optional data) but not the length field itself. A zero-length value is valid and permitted. The SNA message structure remains exactly as defined by the SNA standard; no conversion or modification occurs.

The source UDP port in the Logical Null XID must equal the destination TCP port used later, allowing the receiving node to know which TCP port to expect.
sections.plainLanguage: The setup messages are tiny UDP packets with just a flag. Once connected, each SNA message is preceded by a two-byte number telling TCP how big the message is.

sections.title: Performance and Practical Considerations
sections.content:
Performance measurements comparing SNA/IP to native token-ring LLC showed approximately a 15 percent decrease in maximum transactions per hour (using a test with 1500-byte inbound messages and 50-byte outbound messages). McDATA attributed this to the added processing overhead of TCP/IP in their LinkMaster products compared to LLC in the same devices, not to an inherent limitation of the approach.

SNA/IP can take advantage of class-of-service prioritization already defined by the SNA protocol, allowing applications to request different service levels. It also works with router packet prioritization schemes based on port number, enabling operators to give SNA traffic priority if needed. Future IP technologies offering quality of service (then in development) would further improve SNA/IP performance.
sections.plainLanguage: Running SNA over TCP is a bit slower than using the old local network method, mostly because computers have to do more work. But if you need to cross the Internet, it is the trade-off you make.
